problem.title: Aligning HTTP Keep-Alive Timeouts Across Proxies
problem.prompt: Your checkout web app sits behind an AWS Application Load Balancer (default `idle_timeout = 60s`) and an Nginx ingress (`keepalive_timeout = 65s`), forwarding to Spring Boot Tomcat (`server.tomcat.keep-alive-timeout = 60s`) and a Node.js microservice (`server.keepAliveTimeout = 5s`). Under steady traffic, 0.3% of `POST /orders` requests fail randomly with `502 Bad Gateway` and `upstream prematurely closed connection` / `ECONNRESET` in Nginx/ALB logs—even though backend pods show 0 errors and <20% CPU. Diagnose the TCP race condition and fix the timeout hierarchy.

spark.summary: When a backend's HTTP `keepAliveTimeout` (e.g., 60s) is shorter than or equal to the upstream reverse proxy's idle timeout (e.g., AWS ALB 60s or Nginx 65s), the backend closes the socket with `FIN` at the exact millisecond the proxy reuses it—causing intermittent `502 Bad Gateway` / `ECONNRESET` errors.
spark.keyTakeaway: Always set the backend's `keepAliveTimeout` strictly greater than the upstream proxy's idle timeout (e.g., ALB 60s -> Backend 75s), and let the proxy initiate idle closes.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** In a 3-hop checkout chain (**AWS ALB `idle_timeout = 60s` -> Nginx `keepalive_timeout = 65s` -> Spring Boot Tomcat `60s` / Node.js `5s`**) handling **6,000 RPS** across 30 pods, 0.3% of `POST /orders` calls fail with `502 Bad.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Backend FIN Race (502) vs. Proxy-Initiated Close (AWS ALB (60s) -> Nginx (55s) -> Backend (90s)); Increasing Keep-Alive & Request Limits Downstream (AWS ALB -> Nginx Ingress -> Backend App -> TCP Verify).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Disabling HTTP keep-alive (`Connection: close`) eliminates the race but destroys performance at 6,000 RPS: every request pays a full TCP 3-way handshake + TLS handshake. Enforce a strictly increasing idle-timeout and max-request ladder from edge to origin so the **caller** always closes first: **AWS ALB**: `idle_timeout = 60s` (must be `<` Nginx downstream `keepalive_timeout = 75s`).

**Failure Modes & Application:** Timeout hierarchy alignment is critical across multi-hop cloud topologies: **API Gateways & Ingress Controllers**: Envoy, Nginx, HAProxy, and AWS ALB/NLB pooling to Go, Node.js, or JVM backends.

learningJourney.title: Why HTTP Keep-Alive Timeout Alignment Matters
learningJourney.explanation: In a 3-hop checkout chain (**AWS ALB `idle_timeout = 60s` -> Nginx `keepalive_timeout = 65s` -> Spring Boot Tomcat `60s` / Node.js `5s`**) handling **6,000 RPS** across 30 pods, 0.3% of `POST /orders` calls fail with `502 Bad Gateway` and `ECONNRESET` while backend pods show 0 errors and <20% CPU. Because `POST /orders` is non-idempotent once received by the backend, silent socket drops risk duplicate or lost orders.
learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how Why HTTP Keep-Alive Timeout Alignment Matters works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Real-World Impact of the TCP FIN / RST Race
learningJourney.explanation:
When a downstream server closes an idle keep-alive socket at the exact millisecond an upstream proxy writes a new request onto it:

1. **502 Bad Gateway**: Node.js (`5s`) or Tomcat (`60s`) sends `TCP FIN` while Nginx/ALB simultaneously writes `POST /orders`.
2. **TCP RST Aborts**: The backend kernel replies `TCP RST` to the closed socket; Nginx logs `upstream prematurely closed connection` and returns `502`.
3. **Unsafe Retries**: Because the proxy cannot know whether the backend parsed the `POST` before sending `FIN`, retrying risks double-charging.

learningJourney.title: Naive Solution (and Why It Breaks)
learningJourney.explanation: Disabling HTTP keep-alive (`Connection: close`) eliminates the race but destroys performance at 6,000 RPS: every request pays a full TCP 3-way handshake + TLS handshake, exhausting ephemeral source ports (`TIME_WAIT`) and spiking CPU. Setting equal timeouts (e.g., ALB 60s = Tomcat 60s) still races due to clock drift and timer jitter.
learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Naive Solution under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Enterprise Solution: Strict Downstream Timeout Hierarchy
learningJourney.explanation:
Enforce a strictly increasing idle-timeout and max-request ladder from edge to origin so the **caller** always closes first:

- **AWS ALB**: `idle_timeout = 60s` (must be `<` Nginx downstream `keepalive_timeout = 75s`).
- **Nginx -> Backend Upstream**: Set `keepalive_timeout 55s` and `keepalive_requests 5000` on the Nginx upstream pool.
- **Backend (Tomcat / Node.js)**: Set `server.tomcat.keep-alive-timeout: 90s` (`server.keepAliveTimeout = 90000`, `headersTimeout = 95000` in Node.js) and `max-keep-alive-requests: 10000` so the backend never closes an active pooled connection first.
- **Verification**: Confirm with `tcpdump` that `FIN` packets originate from the proxy, not port 8080.

cards.label: Node.js Pitfall
cards.detail: Node defaults to 5s keepAliveTimeout; must override to 90,000 ms.

sectionDiagram.summary: Every upstream hop closes idle sockets before the downstream server's timer expires, eliminating 502 ECONNRESET races.

learningJourney.title: Where Keep-Alive Alignment Applies in System Design
learningJourney.explanation:
Timeout hierarchy alignment is critical across multi-hop cloud topologies:

- **API Gateways & Ingress Controllers**: Envoy, Nginx, HAProxy, and AWS ALB/NLB pooling to Go, Node.js, or JVM backends.
- **Service Mesh Sidecars**: Istio/Envoy sidecars must have shorter idle timeouts than application servers.
- **gRPC / HTTP/2 Connection Pools**: Aligning `MAX_CONNECTION_IDLE` and `KEEPALIVE_TIME` prevents `GOAWAY` races.
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

options.text: Set Node.js `keepAliveTimeout` strictly greater than Nginx's upstream `keepalive_timeout` (e.g., 90s vs 55s)

_nextProblem.title: Designing Idempotent APIs to Prevent Duplicate Billing
_nextProblem.prompt: Your `billing-service` (Java 21 + PostgreSQL 16 + Redis) processes 2,500 `POST /v1/charges` requests/sec. On flaky 4G mobile networks, a payment succeeds at the card processor (taking 2.1s), but the HTTP response drops before reaching the client. The mobile SDK and Envoy ingress automatically retry `POST /v1/charges` up to 3 times. Because `billing-service` has no idempotency-key enforcement, **0.4% of transactions (10/sec)** are double- or triple-charged, causing $180,000/day in chargebacks and support tickets. Design a strictly consistent, crash-safe idempotency layer that guarantees at-most-once charging even under concurrent identical retries, server crashes mid-flight, and payload-mismatch bugs.

_problemQuestions.prompt: A user edits their bio and refreshes the page, only to see the old bio for 2 seconds because the read hit a lagging replica. Which consistency guarantee was violated?

options.explanation: Read-Your-Writes ensures a client always observes its own completed writes.
The write was durable on the primary; the replica simply lagged.
Atomicity governs all-or-nothing commit, not cross-replica visibility.

_problemQuestions.prompt: Why does placing `request_timestamp` at the very beginning of a 3,000-token system prompt hurt latency and cost?

options.explanation: BPE still tokenizes the text normally.

options.text: It invalidates prefix/KV caching for all subsequent 3,000 tokens on every request
options.explanation: Correct! Prefix KV caching requires an exact token match from index 0 onward.
Output length is unaffected; Prefill cache reuse is what breaks.
